name: Coupling and Cohesion
intent: Judge a design by two measures: how strongly the things inside a module belong together (cohesion) and how much modules know about each other (coupling), and aim for high cohesion and loose coupling where it matters.
scenario: A checkout feature has seven pieces: the checkout flow, the cart, pricing, inventory, billing, notifications and reports. The first version lets them share one mutable state. A second version has each piece call into the internals of the others. A third gives each piece a narrow interface. Then three change requests arrive: a new field in the price structure, a rewrite of the stock logic, and a new signature for the charge call.
problem: Most design principles, from single responsibility to dependency inversion, are ways of improving two properties. Without naming them, advice such as keep it decoupled turns into folklore: some people split everything into tiny pieces, others merge everything to remove dependencies, and neither can say what they gain. Coupling decides how many places a change reaches. Cohesion decides whether a place that changes is small enough to understand and test.

howItWorks.title: Cohesion: do the parts belong together?
howItWorks.text: A module has high cohesion when everything in it serves one purpose and changes for the same reasons: a Pricing module that only prices. It has low cohesion when it is a drawer of unrelated things: a Utils class, or a module that prices, sends email and writes reports. Low cohesion makes a module change for many reasons, and every change forces a re-test of everything in it.

howItWorks.title: Coupling: how much do modules know about each other?
howItWorks.text: Coupling is the degree to which one module depends on another. The classic scale, from loosest to tightest, is: data coupling (only simple values are passed), stamp coupling (a whole structure is passed, when only part of it is needed), control coupling (one module passes a flag that steers the other's logic), common coupling (modules share global or mutable state) and content coupling (one module reaches into another's internals). The tighter the kind, the more kinds of change travel along the dependency.

howItWorks.title: Follow a change to see the blast radius
howItWorks.text: A rewrite of one module's private logic reaches only the modules that reach into its internals. A change to a shared data structure reaches every module that shares or passes it. A change to an operation's signature reaches every caller. The blast radius is the set of modules that must change, plus the ones that must be re-tested because they depend on them. Narrow interfaces keep it small.

howItWorks.title: Talk to friends, not strangers
howItWorks.text: The Law of Demeter says a method should call only its own object's methods, its parameters, objects it creates and its direct parts. A chain such as order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCountry() makes the caller depend on three classes and on how they are linked. A method like order.shippingCountry() lets the structure change behind it. Counting the calls in a chain is a quick smell test, not a rule that every chain is wrong: fluent builders and stream pipelines chain on purpose.

howItWorks.title: Balance the two, and mind the boundary
howItWorks.text: The two measures work together: splitting a module should raise cohesion, and cutting dependencies should lower coupling, but cutting too far makes many tiny modules that all call each other. Tight coupling is fine inside one module, where one person or team owns both sides and they change together. It is expensive across a boundary between teams, services or release cycles, where each side wants to change alone.

pros: A change reaches fewer modules, so it is quicker to make and to review
A cohesive module is easier to name, understand and test on its own
Teams can work and release independently when the modules between them are loosely coupled
Gives a shared vocabulary for judging a design instead of arguing about taste
cons: Loose coupling costs indirection: interfaces, adapters and more files to follow
Both measures are judgement calls: there is no single number, and scores computed from a graph are only a rough guide
Chasing low coupling everywhere can scatter one idea across many tiny modules and hurt cohesion
Some coupling is the point: modules that cooperate must depend on each other somehow
whenToUse: Deciding where to draw a module, service or team boundary
Reviewing a change that unexpectedly touched many files
Judging a refactoring: did the blast radius of the usual changes get smaller?
whenNotToUse: As a metric to maximise on its own, such as a coupling score to push to zero
Inside a small module owned by one person, where tight coupling between its own parts is normal and cheap
Throwaway scripts, where the cost of structure exceeds the cost of change
pitfalls: Reading low coupling as no dependencies at all: modules that work together must depend on something, and the goal is to make the dependency narrow and explicit
Reading high cohesion as one big class: a module with every responsibility has no outside coupling, and every change forces a re-test of all of it
Measuring by file count or lines: ten files that all call into each other's internals are more coupled than one file
Hiding shared mutable state in a global or a singleton: the modules look independent, yet any of them can break the others
Passing a whole object when one field is needed (stamp coupling), so the callee changes whenever the object does
Treating every method chain as a Law of Demeter violation, and wrapping each one in a forwarding method that adds nothing

roles.label: Calling module
roles.description: A module that depends on another to do part of its work.

roles.label: Called module
roles.description: The module that is depended on.

roles.label: Shared state
roles.description: Global or mutable data that several modules read and write.

roles.label: Change request
roles.description: A new requirement that lands in one module and may travel on.

quiz.question: A team removes every dependency between its modules by merging them into one large module. What does this do to coupling and cohesion?
options: Raises both, because a single module has no outside dependencies and everything is together.
Lowers coupling to zero and keeps cohesion unchanged, because the code itself did not change.
Removes the outside coupling but lowers cohesion, so every change still forces a re-test of everything.
Lowers both, because merged modules always depend on one another more tightly than before.
quiz.explanation: Merging hides the dependencies inside one module instead of removing them, and a module with seven responsibilities has low cohesion. A change to any one of them re-tests all seven. High cohesion means the parts belong together, not that there is one part.

quiz.question: Module A reads and writes the same global structure as module B. Which kind of coupling is this, and what follows from it?
options: Data coupling, so a change to B's logic cannot affect A at all.
Common coupling, so a change to the shared structure can affect every module that uses it.
Content coupling, so A can only be changed together with B's private fields.
Control coupling, so A decides which branch B takes with a flag.
quiz.explanation: Sharing global or mutable state is common coupling: tighter than passing a structure and looser than reaching into another module's internals. A change to the shared structure's fields reaches all the modules that use it, even though they never call each other.

quiz.question: A method contains customer.getAddress().getCity().getPostalRules().check(code). What is the most useful way to read this under the Law of Demeter?
options: It is fine, because every call returns an object the method is allowed to use.
It is a bug, because chains of more than two calls fail at run time.
It is only a problem if the chain is written in one line instead of four.
The caller depends on four classes and their links, so the customer should offer a method that answers the question.
quiz.explanation: The caller now changes whenever any class in the chain or the way they connect changes. Asking the nearest object a direct question lets the structure change behind it. Some chains, such as builders or stream pipelines, are fine: they return the same kind of object on purpose.
